content: The content was shared with the relevant stakeholders only after it had undergone a thorough review and revision process by the Guideline Steering Group and the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The primary objective of this step was to gather technical feedback, identify factual inaccuracies, assess the clarity of the language, and provide input on issues related to implementation, adaptation, and contextual considerations. However, the External Review Group was not authorized to alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. Representatives from United Nations agencies were invited to attend the GDG meetings as observers. These representatives had no role in determining the recommendations. The United Nations partners included the Defeat-NCD Partnership (hosted at the United Nations Institute for Training and Research), the International Agency for Research on Cancer, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (hosted at WHO), the United Nations Children’s Fund, the United Nations Development Programme, the United Nations Population Fund, and the World Bank. Additional external partners, also acting as observers without influencing the recommendations, included the International Pharmaceutical Federation, PATH, the Population Council, and the White Ribbon Alliance. All proposed members of the GDG and the External Review Group were required to submit a one-page curriculum vitae and a signed WHO declaration-of-interest form. Two members of the Guideline Steering Group independently reviewed these forms to assess potential conflicts of interest, such as financial ties, academic contributions, or relationships with institutions involved in self-care interventions. The declarations were made publicly available on the WHO website for comment from November 1–16, 2020. GDG members were confirmed only after this process was completed. Once confirmed, all GDG and External Review Group members were instructed to notify the responsible technical officer of any changes in relevant interests during the guideline development process, both before the GDG meeting and prior to submitting comments on a draft version of the guideline. No conflicts of interest were identified that required management or assessment by the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. None of the members had financial conflicts of interest, and the GDG co-chairs also presented no conflicts of interest. A summary of the declarations and information on how conflicts of interest were managed is included in Annex 5. The GDG co-chairs were selected to ensure complementary expertise and perspectives, gender balance, and representation from two different WHO regions. Both co-chairs had relevant expertise in areas pertinent to the guideline and experience in consensus-based processes. The Guideline Steering Group first mapped all existing WHO guidance relevant to self-care, reviewed these materials to identify gaps, overlaps, and inconsistencies, and determined the relevance of existing recommendations for inclusion in the guideline. They also identified areas where new recommendations and key considerations needed to be developed, particularly for sexual and reproductive health and rights. Priority areas for implementation considerations were also identified, including good practice statements on gender and human rights, training of health workers, the use of digital health interventions to support self-care, and priority self-care interventions in humanitarian and pandemic responses. The development of new recommendations began with the formulation of PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions, followed by systematic reviews of the evidence. Eight PICO questions were developed, addressing topics such as self-management of folic acid supplements for pregnancy planning, self-monitoring of blood pressure and glucose during pregnancy, availability of emergency contraceptive pills without a prescription, self-testing for pregnancy, and the use of lubricants to improve sexual health and well-being. Full details of the PICO questions are presented in Annex 6. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Critical outcomes, identified as most important to individuals affected by the guideline, were rated by GDG members via an online survey. Outcomes ranked as critical (scores of 7–9) were included in the GRADE tables to guide decision-making. Following the completion of systematic reviews, GRADE evidence-to-decision tables were prepared for each PICO question. These tables summarized the GDG’s judgments on factors such as benefits and harms, certainty of evidence, values and preferences of end users, resource use, human rights and equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The strength of a recommendation, described as either strong or conditional, reflected the GDG’s confidence in the balance of desirable and undesirable effects. A strong recommendation indicated high confidence that the benefits outweighed the risks, while a conditional recommendation reflected lower certainty or applicability to specific groups or settings. Conditional recommendations were also made when the trade-offs were closely balanced or uncertain, requiring further research to address these uncertainties. The GDG followed a clear decision-making process outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Decisions were ideally made by consensus, but if voting was required, a 60% majority was needed. The GDG reviewed evidence from systematic reviews and GRADE tables, facilitated by the guideline methodologist, and formulated recommendations through group discussion and revision. In an online environment, responses were elicited from all members through straw-polling and chat functions to gauge opinions on the direction and strength of each recommendation. Final wording of recommendations was confirmed by consensus, with all members verbally expressing their decisions. After the GDG meeting, the WHO Guideline Steering Group prepared a draft of the full guideline document, reflecting the deliberations and decisions of the GDG. This draft was sent electronically to GDG members for further comment, and their feedback was integrated before being sent to the External Review Group for input. The Steering Group evaluated the input from the External Review Group for inclusion in the guideline document. Any further modifications were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The revised version was submitted to the Guidelines Review Committee for approval, with minor revisions made before final copy-editing and publication. A list of all reviews conducted for the guideline development, starting with the systematic reviews on the PICO questions, is presented in Annex 6.
